strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: preserving generalization while personalizing federated vision-language models. Keeping modality-specific projections local and aggregating a small shared projection is simple and practically motivated.

The experimental coverage is substantial: eleven datasets, two CLIP backbones, multiple shot counts, and varying client heterogeneity. Reported results include competitive personalization and improved average harmonic-mean accuracy.
Table 18 provides useful evidence for federated sharing: synchronizing the shared projection improves base and novel accuracy over purely local adapters on all six reported datasets.

The communication advantage is quantified. The default configuration exchanges 3,072 parameters in each direction per round versus 8,192 for PromptFL. Reporting training time and memory alongside communication costs is also valuable.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited and insufficiently positioned. The architecture explicitly adopts MMA from Yang et al. (2024), while partitioning parameters into local and globally aggregated components is established in personalized federated learning. The contribution is primarily their combination. The broad claim of being the first adapter-based PFL approach for VLMs also needs reconciliation with the cited FedCLIP work.

Unresolved experimental anomalies undermine confidence. Table 3 reports zero-shot CLIP accuracy of 10.11% on the ten-class DomainNet subset and 9.11% on Office-Caltech10, approximately chance performance. These unexpectedly weak reference results require preprocessing, label-mapping, and prompt sanity checks before the large reported gains are convincing. The collapse of base/novel accuracy at very small residual scaling in Table 5 is also unexplained.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed design. FedCLIP and competitive federated adapter/LoRA alternatives are absent. Although all-global, reversed-sharing, and local-only controls are included, Tables 13 and 18 report different metric subsets under different hyperparameter settings, preventing a complete comparison of personalization–generalization trade-offs. Capacity is another confound: pFedMMA trains approximately 30 times as many parameters as PromptFL.

Several superiority claims overstate the results. In Table 1, average HM improves from PromptFL's 83.09% to 84.15%, a 1.06 percentage-point gain; the highlighted 6.4% relative improvement excludes this stronger baseline. Novel accuracy is only 0.28 points above frozen CLIP. Table 7 shows PromptFL slightly ahead at four shots, and Table 2 shows FedPGP ahead on CIFAR-100 at beta=5 and 10, contradicting claims of consistently highest accuracy.

The domain experiments do not establish unseen-domain generalization: Section 4.1 explicitly states that every domain participates in training and evaluation. They demonstrate performance under heterogeneous observed domains. Using only ten selected DomainNet classes further limits the scope of the robustness conclusions.

Statistical support and reproducibility are insufficient. Three seeds are averaged, but no standard deviations or confidence intervals are reported, making small gains difficult to assess. Adapter initialization, exact class selections, baseline-specific tuning, and validation-based model selection are inadequately documented. Numerical reporting also needs auditing: Table 7 lists two-shot average novel accuracy as 77.37%, whereas its seven dataset entries average approximately 81.60%.
